newsitem.title: GERMANY: Western military set scenarios for Zaire relief.
newsitem.headline: Western military set scenarios for Zaire relief.

text.p: Western military leaders on Sunday agreed on scenarios to help refugees in Zaire that ranged from sending no new troops to using a multinational force to protect the refugees if necessary.

But they did not specify how many troops might be needed under any of the options, which must now go to political leaders for consideration. They also did not say where a mission could be based or what soldiers' rules of engagement might be.

"The mission of a multinational force, as we have defined it, would be to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance and voluntary repatriation of refugees and displaced persons," said General Maurice Baril of Canada, who has been named to head any multinational force.
"The objectives of such a force would be strictly humanitarian. The force would be politically and militarily neutral."
Baril told a news briefing that a three-day meeting of Western and African military leaders in Stuttgart came to a consensus that at least 250,000 refugees were still in eastern Zaire.
This was close to a U.S. estimate released on Saturday of 202,000 but far below estimates of around 700,000 from aid groups and the United Nations High Commission for Refugees.
The meeting, held at U.S. European Command in Germany, concluded that up to 300,000 more refugees may still be in eastern Zaire but that there was no confirmation of this.

The U.N. Security Council approved an armed relief mission to help in the Zaire refugee crisis several weeks ago, but the United States and other nations have become less enthusiastic since the return of some 600,000 refugees to Rwanda in the last 10 days.

Rwanda and the Rwandan-backed Tutsi rebels who have sparked the latest exodus of Rwandan Hutu refugees both say there is no need for a mission as the refugees left in Zaire are either displaced Zaireans or radical Hutus who joined in the 1994 genocide of a million Rwandan Tutsis.
A discussion paper seen by Reuters at the meeting set out the pros and cons of basing the mission in Rwanda or in Zaire.
Baril made no mention of where any operation would be based and said he was "concerned about opposition to the mission".
But he added: "I am pretty sure that we can make those involved understand that we are on a humanitarian operation."
He also said that he had secured an agreement from Rwanda's military strongman, Vice-President Paul Kagame, to let any multinational humanitarian force transit the country.
Baril declined to specify the size of any force, whose mandate would run to March 31, 1997.

Eight potential contributors, including the United States, France, Canada, Spain and Britain, attended Sunday's final session. But some 15 others, including African countries, attended the first two days of the meeting on Friday and Saturday.
Canadian Commander Barry Frewer, the designated spokesman for the mission, said the intention was not to put troops into Zaire "while there is fighting on the ground".
But he declined to say whether any of the options to be offered to governments included overcoming resistance from the Zairean Tutsi rebels.
Frewer said he could envisage, under the most forceful of the four options, that troops might secure food depots in Zaire so that refugees would be able approach them with confidence.
Baril defined this option as aiding "humanitarian assistance and voluntary repatriation of refugees in an environment in which security forces would be required for protection".
The discussion papers at the meeting said providing relief from a base in Rwanda would need only light security.
It said providing relief from a Zairean base would mean establishing a secure headquarters, probably with heavy forces, and carry a bigger risk of becoming embroiled in conflict.
Such a mission would also need more complex logistical support than a Rwanda-based operation and take more time.
